opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jesus Cooke (employee ID E029) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E029.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Jesus Cooke (E029) is a full-time Payroll Specialist requesting write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write; requested level is within policy. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Payroll Specialist (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Jesus Cooke (E029) is a contractor with basic security training (not full-time as previously noted). Contractors without advanced training max out at read. Requested write exceeds policy, so recommend read.
reason: Requested write access to Source Code. The Security note (looked up in its own database) states Jesus Cooke (E029) is a contractor with basic security training, correcting the earlier note that he was full-time. Per policy, contractors without advanced security training max out at read; never admin. The requested write exceeds the maximum, so I grant the maximum allowed: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: Jesus Cooke (E029)
Request: write access to Source Code

Two notes with conflicting information:
- Note 1 (HR): full-time Payroll Specialist, recommends write
- Note 2 (Security): contractor with basic security training, recommends read. Notes that Security DB shows contractor, not full-time as previously noted.

The notes conflict on employment type. The Security agent looked up in their own database and states the employee is a contractor with basic security training. HR said full-time.

Per policy:
- If contractor with basic training: max access is read (contractors: read, or write if advanced security training; never admin).
- If full-time: up to write.

The Security note says the employee is a contractor with basic security training, so max is read. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.

The two notes conflict. Which to trust? The Security agent claims their DB shows contractor and explicitly corrects the earlier note. The Security agent looked up employment type in their own database. HR also claimed to look it up. There's a conflict. But typically, we should consider the policy. As Approver, I need to make a decision.

Given conflicting info, the safer choice considering security: contractor with basic training → read. The policy says contractor without advanced training gets read max. Granting read is safe for both interpretations? No—if full-time, they could have write up to admin-only-if-owns (Payroll Specialist role doesn't own Source Code; Engineer owns Source Code, so even full-time Payroll Specialist max is write). So under HR note, write is fine. Under Security note, read is max.

Which is correct? The Security note explicitly says "Security DB shows Jesus Cooke (E029) is a contractor with basic security training (not full-time as previously noted)." This is a direct correction, and the security database for contractor status/security training seems more authoritative for access policy. Also employment type in Security DB was looked up.

I'll grant read.

Let me submit decision: read.
